newsitem.title: MEXICO: Leftist leader accuses Mexico ruling party of fraud.
newsitem.headline: Leftist leader accuses Mexico ruling party of fraud.

text.p: The leader of Mexico's main leftist opposition accused President Ernesto Zedillo's party on Thursday of voter fraud to help keep its 68-year-old congressional majority in key elections next month.
"They (the PRI) are intensifying vote buying," Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, president of the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), told Reuters in an interview.
"They are trafficking with the needy and the poverty of the people, handing out food parcels and construction materials," he added.

Government officials have strongly denied any misuse of public funds in the campaign for elections on July 6. But Lopez Obrador said the PRD intended to put observers in every one of the 100,000 voting booths to stop possible fraud.
He strongly attacked Zedillo for acting as "PRI campaign chief" instead of pushing for greater democracy for his country, which has been ruled by the PRI since 1929.
"Zedillo has no democratic vocation," the PRD leader charged. "It is very regrettable ... in Mexico there has never been democracy but we have never been so close to achieving it."

In the July elections, which come halfway through Zedillo's six-year term, Mexicans will choose a new lower house of congress, a quarter of the Senate and six state governors as well as the first elected mayor of Mexico City.
Government officials say recent electoral reforms have eliminated Mexico's long and ugly tradition of voting fraud.
The changes include one of the world's most elaborate electoral lists featuring photographs of every voter as well as an independent electoral authority.
But Lopez Obrador claimed some rural areas of Mexico were still controlled by old-style bosses linked to the PRI.

"We know well that if we don't have representatives in those booths (the PRI) will help themselves with a big spoon -- that's to say up to 90 percent of the electoral list will 'vote' in favour of the PRI," he said.
Under Mexico's electoral rules, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) needs just over 42 percent of the national vote to keep its majority in the lower house.
PRI leaders claim they will win that level of support but some polls have shown the party below that threshold.
Lopez Obrador, who has spent the past months campaigning across the country, predicted that "if the elections are clean and free, the PRI won't even reach 35 percent".

He put PRD support at a minimum of 25 percent -- well up on the 16.6 percent the party achieved in 1994. Polls suggest that the conservative National Action Party (PAN) is likely to be the other major player, winning around 30 percent.
